meta.title: Who originally recorded "Try a Little Tenderness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Otis Redding. The song was published in London in November 1932 and cut by British dance bands within weeks — the earliest documented session is Jack Payne and His Band, though sources disagree.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Try a Little Tenderness'?
meta.ogDescription: Otis Redding's 1966 Stax version is definitive, not original. The song was published in London in November 1932 and the earliest documented recording is Jack Payne and His Band.

answer.label: Not an Otis Redding original — the song is a 1932 British dance-band number, and the earliest documented recording is Jack Payne and His Band, London, November 1932
answer.originalArtistDates: Jack Payne, 1899-1969, English bandleader and the BBC’s first Director of Dance Music
answer.sourceLine: Otis Redding’s 1966 Volt single is so total a performance that it reads as an origin, but the song was published in London on 4 November 1932, written by Harry M. Woods with Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly. Three British dance bands were on it within weeks. The earliest documented session is Jack Payne and His Band, cut in London in November 1932 with Payne himself singing and issued on Imperial 2792 — a dating that rests on Brian Rust and Sandy Forbes’s British Dance Bands on Record 1911-1945, the standard reference discography for this repertoire, as cited with the archive transfer of the disc. Then come Carroll Gibbons and the Savoy Hotel Orpheans on 1 December 1932 (Columbia CB-546), and only then the Ray Noble Orchestra with Val Rosing on 8 December 1932. We flag this page as disputed because Wikipedia still names the Noble session as the first recording and does not mention Payne at all; the specialist discographies say otherwise, and we have not been able to put a day-of-month on the Payne date. What is not in doubt is the direction of travel: whoever reached the microphone first, it was a British dance band in 1932, not Otis Redding.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Imperial (UK)
original.released: Recorded in London in November 1932 by Jack Payne and His Band, with Payne taking the vocal himself, and issued as a 78rpm single on Imperial 2792 in January 1933, backed with “When the Morning Rolls Around”. Payne had left the BBC Dance Orchestra earlier in 1932 and moved his recording to Imperial.
original.charted: No chart placing is documented for any of the 1932 British recordings — Britain had no record chart until 1952. The song’s first documented American hits came in 1933, with Ted Lewis and Ruth Etting.
original.writer: Harry M. Woods, Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly
original.cover: Otis Redding, recorded at Stax in Memphis in 1966 with Booker T. & the M.G.’s and Isaac Hayes on the arrangement. Released on Volt/Atco V-141 and on Complete & Unbelievable: The Otis Redding Dictionary of Soul; it peaked at No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100 and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2015.

trail: Brian Rust and Sandy Forbes, British Dance Bands on Record 1911-1945 — the standard reference discography for this repertoire — is cited with the archive transfer of the Payne disc as dating his session ahead of both the Carroll Gibbons and Ray Noble recordings. The transfer comes from the Charles Hippisley-Cox British Dance Band Collection held at Heritage Quay, the University of Huddersfield archive. This is the strongest evidence on the page, and it is the reason the Wikipedia line no longer leads.

45cat’s entry for Imperial 2792 ↗ confirms the issue: Jack Payne, “Try a Little Tenderness” backed with “When the Morning Rolls Around”, January 1933 — consistent with a session in the previous November.

A discography devoted to the British dance-band singer Maurice Elwin dates a Carroll Gibbons and Savoy Hotel Orpheans session ↗ to 1 December 1932 in London, Columbia CB-546. It lists Jack Payne among the bands that recorded the song in 1932-33 but makes no claim about who was first.

Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗ gives the publication date of 4 November 1932 by Campbell, Connelly & Co., Ltd., and states that the first recording was the Ray Noble Orchestra’s of 8 December 1932 with Val Rosing. Val Rosing’s article ↗ repeats it — but both are Wikipedia, so that is one tertiary source stated twice, not two sources, and the specialist discographies outrank it.
MusicBrainz ↗ carries the Ray Noble recording attached to the February 1933 US Victor release pairing it with Don Bestor’s “Close to Your Heart”.

authors.name: Jack Payne and His Band
authors.heading: Jack Payne & his Band
authors.metaLine: Jack Payne, 1899-1969 - English bandleader, the BBC’s first Director of Dance Music
authors.bio: Jack Payne ↗ — born John Wesley Vivian Payne in Leamington Spa — ran the BBC Dance Orchestra from 1928, which made him the most heard bandleader in Britain and put him in the first BBC television broadcast in 1929. He left the BBC in 1932, took his band on the road and moved his recording to Imperial, which is how the earliest known reading of this song came to be a house-band leader singing his own vocal on a cheap label in November 1932. Rust and Forbes’s standard discography of British dance bands places that session ahead of both Carroll Gibbons’s and Ray Noble’s. The performance is brisk and unsentimental, the title taken as advice rather than as an appeal.

authors.name: Otis Redding
authors.heading: Otis Redding
authors.bio: Redding recorded the song at Stax in Memphis in 1966 with Booker T. & the M.G.’s, Isaac Hayes shaping the arrangement, and released it on Volt/Atco V-141 and on Complete & Unbelievable: The Otis Redding Dictionary of Soul. He rebuilt it from the ground up: a slow, almost hymnal opening that escalates into an unstoppable finish. It peaked at No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100, entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2015 and sits at No. 136 on Rolling Stone’s 500 Greatest Songs list. The only error anyone makes about it is chronological.

authors.name: Harry M. Woods, Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly
authors.heading: Woods, Campbell & Connelly
authors.metaLine: Harry M. Woods, 1896-1970, American; Jimmy Campbell, 1903-1967 and Reg Connelly, 1895-1963, English
authors.bio: Harry M. Woods ↗ was a Tin Pan Alley composer whose catalogue includes “When the Red, Red Robin Comes Bob, Bob, Bobbin’ Along” and “Side by Side”; he was born with a deformed left hand and was pushed toward the piano by his mother, a concert singer. Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly ↗ were English songwriters and publishers who had worked together since about 1925 and founded the firm Campbell Connelly in 1929 — the same partnership behind “Show Me the Way to Go Home” and “Goodnight Sweetheart”. Their company published this song on 4 November 1932.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The famous version is a cover of a pre-war British standard. The only genuinely open question is which 1932 dance band recorded it first.

items.who: Otis Redding wrote or originated it
items.why: Redding’s recording is a 1966 Stax reading of a song published in London in November 1932. He did not write it and was not the first to record it.

items.who: Jack Payne and His Band, London, November 1932
items.why: Rust and Forbes’s British Dance Bands on Record 1911-1945, cited with the archive transfer of the disc, places Payne ahead of both December sessions. Issued on Imperial 2792 in January 1933. We have a month, not a day, which is why the page stays marked disputed.

items.who: Carroll Gibbons and the Savoy Hotel Orpheans, 1 December 1932
items.why: A specialist discography dates a London session with Maurice Elwin and the Carlyle Cousins to 1 December 1932, Columbia CB-546. It does not itself claim to be the first.

items.who: Ray Noble Orchestra, vocal by Val Rosing, 8 December 1932
items.why: Wikipedia calls this the first recording, issued on HMV B-6284 and on Victor 24263 in America in February 1933, and does not mention Payne or Gibbons. It is the most widely repeated answer and the most easily checked, but on the discographical evidence it is the third documented recording.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a 1932 British dance-band song. The earliest documented recording is Jack Payne’s, in November 1932, with Carroll Gibbons and Ray Noble following in December — and Otis Redding, who was born in 1941, was never in the running.

context.heading: How a 1932 dance-band number became a soul monument
lead: The interesting question is not why people forget the 1932 record — it is why Otis Redding’s version erased not one predecessor but dozens. Between its publication in London in November 1932 and Redding’s Memphis session, the song had been through Ted Lewis, Ruth Etting, Bing Crosby, Frank Sinatra twice, and a whole shelf of British dance bands. It was a well-worn standard, the kind of thing an artist picks up because everybody already knows it.

What Redding and Isaac Hayes did was change the song’s grammar. The 1932 arrangements treat the title as gentle advice, delivered at a tempo you could dance to in a hotel ballroom. The Stax version treats it as something the singer has to survive, starting almost motionless and ending at full sprint, with Booker T. & the M.G.’s pushing the floor out from under it. When a performance reorganises a song that completely, the earlier readings stop sounding like versions of the same thing — which is exactly how an origin gets overwritten.
detailsBody: 4 November 1932 — the song is published in London by Campbell, Connelly & Co., Ltd., music by Harry M. Woods, lyrics by Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly.

November 1932 — Jack Payne and His Band record it in London, Payne singing, issued on Imperial 2792 in January 1933. Rust and Forbes’s standard British dance-band discography, cited with the archive transfer of the disc, places this ahead of both December sessions. It is the earliest documented recording we can find, though no day of the month is given.
1 December 1932 — a specialist discography dates a London session by Carroll Gibbons and the Savoy Hotel Orpheans, vocals by Maurice Elwin and the Carlyle Cousins, issued on Columbia CB-546.

8 December 1932 — the Ray Noble Orchestra records it with Val Rosing on vocal. Issued on HMV B-6284 in Britain and, in February 1933, on Victor 24263 in America. This is the session Wikipedia still calls the first recording.
9 January 1933 — Bing Crosby records it for Brunswick.
1933 — Ted Lewis (Columbia 2748 D) and Ruth Etting (Melotone 12625) have hits with it in the United States.
1946 and 1960 — Frank Sinatra records it twice, keeping it in circulation as a ballad standard.

1966 — Otis Redding records it at Stax with Booker T. & the M.G.’s and Isaac Hayes; released on Volt/Atco V-141 and on Complete & Unbelievable: The Otis Redding Dictionary of Soul. It reaches No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100.
1969 — Three Dog Night’s version reaches No. 29 on the Billboard Hot 100.
context.pull: It was a thirty-four-year-old standard when Stax got hold of it.

schema.faqAnswer: No. "Try a Little Tenderness" was published in London in November 1932, written by Harry M. Woods, Jimmy Campbell and Reg Connelly, and recorded by British dance bands within weeks. The earliest documented session is Jack Payne and His Band, London, November 1932, issued on Imperial 2792; Carroll Gibbons recorded it on 1 December 1932 and Ray Noble on 8 December 1932. Which was first is disputed — Wikipedia names Ray Noble, the specialist discographies name Jack Payne. Otis Redding's 1966 Stax version is a cover.
